ABOLISHED HEART-BALM ACTIONS IN CALIFORNIA — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

DECLARATION OF PARTIES AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Abolished Heart-Balm Actions in California — Information Sheet concerns Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee. It describes what California statute says about a group of civil lawsuits — historically called "heart-balm" actions — that a person can no longer bring in California based on the end of a courtship, engagement, or marriage: alienation of affection, criminal conversation, seduction of a person over the age of legal consent, and breach of promise of marriage. It also describes a separate, related statute that lets a person who gave a gift of money or property because a marriage was expected seek the gift's return, or the value a court or jury finds just, when the marriage does not take place. This information sheet states general legal facts about these statutes. It does not determine, and takes no position on, whether any claim by Jordan Alex Lee or Morgan Casey Lee is barred, available, or would succeed; that depends on the specific facts and, if disputed, is for a court to decide.

FOUR NAMED CAUSES OF ACTION NO LONGER EXIST UNDER CALIFORNIA LAW
California statute provides that no cause of action arises for four named claims: alienation of affection; criminal conversation; seduction of a person over the age of legal consent; and breach of promise of marriage. The statute bars all four by name in a single list, without conditioning the bar on which party was at fault, how long the relationship lasted, or whether a wedding date had been set.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "No cause of action arises for: (a) Alienation of affection. (b) Criminal conversation. (c) Seduction of a person over the age of legal consent. (d) Breach of promise of marriage."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 43.5 (California Legislative Information text), no cause of action arises for four named claims (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=43.5.)
  Known gap: This clause states only that Civil Code section 43.5 bars a cause of action under each of these four names; the statute itself does not define any of the four terms it uses, so what conduct historically fell within "alienation of affection," "criminal conversation," "seduction," or "breach of promise of marriage" is not stated in this text. CourtListener's case-law search was attempted for this document and returned a rate-limit error (125/day exhausted) before any pre-1939 or later California decision construing these terms could be fetched and verified this session, so no case law defining these terms is cited anywhere in this document.

ALIENATION OF AFFECTION AND CRIMINAL CONVERSATION ARE BARRED
Among the four claims the statute bars are alienation of affection and criminal conversation. These two were historically directed at a third party rather than at a spouse or partner directly — alienation of affection at someone accused of damaging a marriage, and criminal conversation, despite its name, at someone accused of having a sexual relationship with a person's spouse. California statute states that no cause of action arises for either one.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) Alienation of affection. (b) Criminal conversation."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 43.5(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), alienation of affection and criminal conversation barred (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=43.5.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the two-item list; it does not itself state which third party, if any, could historically have been sued, what evidence such a claim required, or how the tort of criminal conversation — a civil claim despite its name — differed from any criminal statute. No case law defining these two torts as they existed before the 1939 bar was fetched or verified this session.

SEDUCTION OF A PERSON OVER THE AGE OF LEGAL CONSENT IS BARRED
California statute also bars a cause of action for seduction of a person over the age of legal consent. The bar is limited by its own terms to a person over that age; this section does not use the word "seduction" anywhere else, and it does not itself state what age counts as the age of legal consent.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(c) Seduction of a person over the age of legal consent."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 43.5(c) (California Legislative Information text), seduction of a person over the age of legal consent barred (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=43.5.)
  Known gap: This clause states only that the statute bars a claim labeled "seduction of a person over the age of legal consent"; it does not identify which other California statute sets that age, and it does not address a claim involving a person under that age, which this section does not purport to cover one way or the other. No case law was fetched or verified for this clause this session.

BREACH OF PROMISE OF MARRIAGE IS BARRED
The fourth claim the statute bars is breach of promise of marriage — historically a lawsuit for damages when one person called off an expected wedding after promising to marry the other. California statute states that no cause of action arises for breach of promise of marriage, without an exception based on how far wedding planning had progressed or which party ended the engagement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(d) Breach of promise of marriage."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 43.5(d) (California Legislative Information text), breach of promise of marriage barred (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=43.5.)
  Known gap: This clause addresses only the cause of action for damages based on a broken promise to marry; it does not address, and this section does not by its own text speak to, a separate question covered by a different statute — the return of a specific gift given because a marriage was expected. That separate question is addressed in the companion clauses of this information sheet describing Civil Code section 1590.

A SEPARATE STATUTE LETS A DONOR SEEK RETURN OF A GIFT GIVEN BECAUSE MARRIAGE WAS EXPECTED
A different Civil Code section, enacted the same year as the bar on breach-of-promise lawsuits, addresses gifts given because a marriage was expected. It states that where either party to a contemplated marriage in California makes a gift of money or property to the other on the basis or assumption that the marriage will take place, and the marriage does not happen because the donee refuses to go through with it or because it is called off by mutual consent, the donor may recover the gift.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Where either party to a contemplated marriage in this State makes a gift of money or property to the other on the basis or assumption that the marriage will take place, in the event that the donee refuses to enter into the marriage as contemplated or that it is given up by mutual consent, the donor may recover such gift"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1590 (California Legislative Information text), donor may recover a gift given because marriage was expected (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1590.)
  Known gap: This clause states only that a recovery right exists under the statute's own terms — it does not address a marriage that is called off unilaterally by the donor rather than the donee, or called off in circumstances outside the two categories the statute names, does not address gifts made after (rather than in contemplation of) a wedding, and does not state a limitations period within which a donor must act. No California case applying this section — for example, to a specific engagement ring — was fetched or verified this session.

THE AMOUNT RECOVERABLE IS WHATEVER A COURT OR JURY FINDS JUST, NOT AUTOMATICALLY THE FULL GIFT
The same statute does not state that a donor automatically recovers the entire gift or its full value. Instead, the statute allows recovery of "such gift or such part of its value" as a court or jury finds, under all the circumstances of the case, to be just.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "or such part of its value as may, under all of the circumstances of the case, be found by a court or jury to be just."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1590 (California Legislative Information text), recoverable amount is what a court or jury finds just (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1590.)
  Known gap: This clause states only the statutory standard — that the amount is left to a finding of what is "just" under the circumstances of the case — it does not itself list what circumstances a court or jury may consider, and no case law applying this discretionary standard to a specific set of facts was fetched or verified this session.

BOTH STATUTES TRACE TO THE SAME 1939 LEGISLATIVE ACT
The statute barring alienation of affection, criminal conversation, seduction, and breach-of-promise lawsuits, and the separate statute allowing a donor to recover a gift given because a marriage was expected, were both added to the Civil Code by the same legislative act, identified in the statutory text of each section as Statutes 1939, Chapter 128.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(Added by Stats. 1939, Ch. 128.)"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 43.5 (California Legislative Information text), enactment history line for section 43.5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=43.5.)
  "(Added by Stats. 1939, Ch. 128.)"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1590 (California Legislative Information text), enactment history line for section 1590 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1590.)
  Known gap: This clause states only that both sections carry the identical enactment citation appended to their current text on the California Legislative Information website; it does not itself establish, and this document takes no position on, the Legislature's purpose in enacting the two sections together, nor whether either section has been amended since 1939 in ways not reflected in the "Added by" line each section currently displays. No legislative history document, such as a bill analysis, was fetched or reviewed for this clause.

THE BAR IS LIMITED BY ITS TEXT TO THE FOUR NAMED CLAIMS
The statute's operative sentence bars a cause of action only under the four labels it lists. It does not state that it bars any other kind of civil claim that might arise from the same events, such as a claim based on a contract, a claim to recover specific property, or a claim of fraud.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "No cause of action arises for:"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 43.5 (California Legislative Information text), the bar is stated as a list of four named claims (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=43.5.)
  Known gap: This clause describes only what the statute's text does say — that it names four specific causes of action — and does not itself say what other causes of action, if any, might be available on the same underlying facts; the statute is silent on that question, and no California case addressing the boundary between the four barred claims and other legal theories was fetched or verified this session, because CourtListener's search quota was exhausted (125/day) when this document was researched.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT — NOT A COURT FILING
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

A person who needs a determination for a specific set of facts should consult the applicable statutes and, if the matter is disputed, the court.]
